options.text: A metaphor comparing maintenance to rest.
A literal description of the closure.
A euphemism that softens the reality of a closure.
An anaphora repeating 'period'.

questions.explanation: The phrase softens a closure, which is euphemism. Reading it literally misses the softening.
questions.hint: Soft words for a hard change.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Stance carried by a single word in a report
questions.stem: The report calls the new coach 'experimental'; explain the stance this single word carries.

answer.exemplar: The word 'experimental' carries a cautious, doubtful stance toward the new coach, colouring the whole report.

questions.explanation: One loaded word can carry stance. Treating it as neutral ignores the diction.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Purpose signalled in the opening of a letter
questions.stem: A letter opens 'I am writing to apologise for the delay'; what purpose is signalled?

options.text: The purpose is to inform only.
The purpose is to confirm the delay.
The purpose is to thank the club.
The purpose is to apologise for the delay.

questions.explanation: The opening states the purpose directly. Reading a confirmation into it confuses purpose with topic.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Building a thesis with three criteria

stimulus.body: The club must choose a new hall. Cost, access and capacity matter. A good thesis names all three. The reader should see the criteria clearly.

questions.stem: Which thesis best uses cost, access and capacity as criteria?

options.text: The hall is cheap, so it is good enough.
The hall is justified by low cost, easy access and large capacity.
The hall looks nice, which is all that matters.
options.misconception: overstates the claim in the summary

options.text: The hall is new, so it must be better.

questions.explanation: A thesis with three criteria names all three. Omitting criteria leaves the argument incomplete.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: A conclusion that adds rather than repeats
questions.stem: A club report ends 'so the hall pays for itself in three seasons'; what does this conclusion do?

options.text: It introduces an unrelated topic.
It repeats the opening sentence verbatim.
It adds a new point about payback instead of repeating.
It merely lists the costs again.

questions.explanation: The conclusion adds a payback point. Calling it a repeat confuses adding with restating.
questions.hint: A good conclusion extends, not repeats.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Comparing two passages on one subject
questions.stem: Compare two club passages about the same hall; explain what the reader should focus on.

answer.exemplar: The reader should focus on how each passage's stance and evidence differ, since both discuss the same hall.

questions.explanation: Comparison centres on stance and substance. Counting words or dates misses the point.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Screening joins for the relation they claim
questions.stem: A club email joins two clauses with 'therefore'; what relation does it claim?

options.text: A temporal sequence only.
A contrast between the clauses.
A mere listing of two facts.
A consequential relation between the clauses.

questions.explanation: 'Therefore' claims consequence. Reading it as a mere list ignores the relation.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Screening inferences for what a notice licenses

stimulus.body: The club notice says the cafe closes at seven. It gives no other information. The reader should infer only what is stated. Nothing about staffing is said.

questions.stem: What does the notice license and not license?

options.text: It licenses that the club is short of staff.
It licenses that the cafe closes at seven, not staffing reasons.
It licenses that hours will change soon.
It licenses nothing at all.
options.misconception: reads stance from facts not diction

questions.explanation: A notice licenses only what it states. Inferring staffing or future changes goes beyond it.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Asking for the main idea
questions.stem: A club article lists five match results, then ends 'so focus, not flair, needs work'; what is the main idea?

options.text: The list should be shortened next time.
Five matches were played this month.
Focus, not flair, needs work.
Flair scores are stable overall.
options.misconception: reads stance from facts not diction

questions.explanation: The final clause states the point. Treating the results list as the point confuses detail with conclusion.
questions.hint: The point sits after the list.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Asking for a detail
questions.stem: The club notice states the pool closes at eight, the gym at nine and the cafe at seven; state one detail it gives.

answer.exemplar: The notice states that the gym closes at nine, one clear detail a reader can check.

questions.explanation: The notice gives specific closing times per facility. Mixing them up would misread the detail.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Translating a sentence while keeping its register
questions.stem: A club email says 'Dans l'attente de votre reponse'; which English keeps the formal register?

options.text: You must reply now.
options.misconception: reads stance from facts not diction

options.text: Waiting to hear back from you.
options.misconception: uses informal register in formal text

options.text: Reply soon, please.
Awaiting your reply, we remain at your service.

questions.explanation: The formal French calls for polite English. The blunt option drops the register.
questions.hint: Match the formality of the source.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Counterclaim and concession

stimulus.body: The club report argues for a new track, then admits the ground is soft. The admission is brief. The main claim stands. The reader should notice the concession.

questions.stem: What does the admission 'the ground is soft' function as?

options.text: A counterclaim that replaces the main claim.
options.misconception: misses the concession in the clause

options.text: A concession that strengthens the claim by acknowledging a drawback.
A summary of the whole report.
options.misconception: overstates the claim in the summary

options.text: A detail with no argumentative role.

questions.explanation: The admission grants a point while the main claim stands. Calling it a replacement misses the concession.
questions.hint: An admission keeping the claim is a concession.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Summary against list
questions.stem: A club memo lists five drills, then ends 'so balance, not speed, is the gap'; is the final clause a summary?

options.text: No, it merely repeats the drill names.
No, it adds a new unrelated claim.
options.misconception: overstates the claim in the summary

options.text: Yes, it compresses the list into one point.
Yes, because it lists the drills again.
options.misconception: reads stance from facts not diction

questions.explanation: The final clause compresses the list into one point. Calling it a new claim ignores the compression.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: A transition that names the relationship
questions.stem: The club report uses 'nevertheless' between two paragraphs; explain what relationship it names.

answer.exemplar: 'Nevertheless' names a concessive relation, signalling that the second paragraph holds despite the first.

questions.explanation: The transition names concession. Reading it as addition misses the opposition.
